h1: From hotel management to taproom manager: the career path
title: Hotel Management to Taproom Manager | Craft Beer School
desc: How hotel management graduates move into taproom and brewpub management in India: transferable skills, beer knowledge to add and how to get hired.
teaser: You trained to run a floor, a kitchen and a team. A taproom needs all of that, plus someone who understands the beer.
standfirst: Hotel management graduates already have most of what a brewpub needs in a floor manager. This guide shows what carries over, what you need to learn about beer and how to make the move.
sections:
A brewpub is a restaurant with a brewery inside it. The brewery makes the product, but the floor makes the money. Owners need managers who can run service, control costs, train staff, handle complaints and keep the place full on a Tuesday as well as a Saturday.

Hotel management training covers exactly this: food and beverage service, kitchen operations, cost control, hygiene and staff management. Many brewpub managers in India come from hotels and restaurants rather than from brewing. Our guide to taproom economics shows why the floor matters so much to the numbers.

• Service standards: greeting, order flow, table turns and handling difficult guests.
  • Cost control: food cost, beverage cost, wastage and stock counts.
  • Staff management: rosters, training, appraisals and keeping a team motivated through late shifts.
  • Hygiene and safety: food safety systems and licence inspections.
  • Events: planning private parties, launches and corporate bookings.

These are the skills owners struggle to find in brewers. You already have them.
What you need to learn about beer

The gap is product knowledge. A taproom manager should be able to explain every beer on the board, recommend a beer to a guest who says they do not like beer and tell when a beer is pouring badly.

Start with the basics: how beer is made, the main styles and what makes each one different. Learn the draught system, because foamy pours and warm beer waste money and annoy guests. Understand freshness: hoppy beers fade within weeks and the Indian heat speeds that up. Spend time with the brewer, taste every batch and ask questions. Our beer styles guide is a good place to begin.
The marketing side of the job

In a hotel, marketing usually sits with a separate team. In a brewpub, the taproom manager is often the marketing team. You may run the brewpub's Instagram, plan events, organise beer launches, build a regulars' community and work with delivery apps where they are allowed.

This is where many hospitality people find a gap. A taproom lives on repeat visits. Repeat visits come from giving people a reason to return: new beers, events, a sense that they belong. Planning a monthly calendar of launches, quiz nights and food pairings is part of the job. Rules on alcohol advertising in India are strict and vary by state, so learn what your outlet may and may not promote before you post.

Most people move in at assistant manager or floor manager level, often after a few years in hotel or restaurant operations. Brewpubs in Bengaluru, Pune, Mumbai, Gurugram and Hyderabad hire regularly.

To stand out, show you understand the business. In an interview, talk about how you would raise beer sales per cover, cut wastage or fill quiet weekdays. Mention that you know the brewery side matters: that you would work with the brewer on the tap list and keep the lines clean. A candidate who has visited the brewpub, tasted the beers and has two or three ideas is ahead of most applicants.
What a typical shift looks like

A taproom manager's day often starts in the afternoon. You check the cold room and the tap list with the brewer, confirm which kegs are running low and brief the floor team on any new beer. During service you watch the pours, handle tables with problems and keep an eye on the till. After closing you count stock, reconcile sales and check that the lines and glassware are clean.

The hours are long and weekends are the busiest days. Hotel people are used to that. The difference is the product: you spend part of every shift tasting and talking about beer, which is the reason many people make the move.

From taproom manager the path usually leads to general manager of a brewpub, operations manager across several outlets or a business development role opening new locations. Some people move into brand and marketing roles for breweries, using what they learned about guests on the floor.

Others go into partnership or open their own place. Hospitality people who also understand beer and community make strong founders, because they know where the money is made.

1. Learn how beer is made and the main styles.
  2. Taste every beer on the tap list and write notes.
  3. Learn to clean and balance a draught system.
  4. Understand the cost of each pour and the margin.
  5. Plan a month of events for an imaginary brewpub.
  6. Learn the local rules on alcohol promotion.

The first four you can learn from the brewer. The last two are where a structured approach to taproom marketing and community building helps most.
faqs: Do brewpubs prefer hotel management graduates?
Many brewpub floor and general managers come from hotel and restaurant backgrounds, because the service, cost and staff skills transfer directly. Beer knowledge is then added on the job.
Do I need to know how to brew to manage a taproom?
No, but you should understand how beer is made, the styles on your board and how the draught system works. Spending time with the brewer helps.
Is marketing part of a taproom manager's job?
In most Indian brewpubs, yes. Events, social media and community building often sit with the taproom manager rather than a separate team.
